Field guide · goals, agents, loops

Orchestrating Claude

How to give Claude a goal it can check, let it explore and plan with helper agents, make it prove its own work, and keep it running when you step away. Plain words, with a picture for every moving part. Advice from Boris Cherny (who created Claude Code), Andrej Karpathy, Anthropic's engineers and leading practitioners is tagged by how solid its source is.

The whole idea in one line

You own the goal and the bar for done. Claude runs the loop until it clears the bar, or stops and asks you.

Words you'll meet goal, check, context window, subagent, orchestrator, hook, Stop hook, harness, receipt, worktree, MCP, headless, sandbox, lethal trifecta
goal
What you want done, how you will know it is done, and the limits Claude works within. Lesson 1
check, gate
A test, command or observation that decides if the work is done. A gate runs one automatically, so Claude can't skip it. Lesson 1
context window
Claude's working memory. Every file it reads fills it, and when it gets full, early details fade. Lesson 2
subagent, helper
A helper agent that does one narrow job in its own context window and sends back a short summary. Lesson 1
orchestrator, lead
The main Claude session. It holds the goal and plan, makes the calls, and hands jobs to helpers. That is orchestration. Lesson 1
hook
A script of yours that runs on its own when a set event happens, so Claude can't skip it. Lesson 1
Stop hook
A hook that runs when Claude tries to finish, for example to rerun the tests. It can block Claude from finishing. Lesson 2
harness
Everything wrapped around the model to steer it: its tools, rules and checks. Each piece should prevent a named failure. Lesson 2
receipt
A closing report: each check from your goal marked PASS, FAIL or NOT RUN, with the command behind it. Lesson 4
worktree
A separate copy of your project's code, so two agents never edit the same files. Lesson 6
MCP
Short for Model Context Protocol. Plug-ins that connect Claude to outside tools such as GitHub, Linear and browsers. Lesson 8
headless
Claude running with no chat window, called from a script (claude -p) instead of you typing to it. Lesson 10
sandbox
A restricted space for shell commands, limiting the files and network they can reach. Edits, hooks and MCP servers run outside it. Lesson 7
lethal trifecta
An agent that holds private data, reads untrusted content and can send data out can be steered into leaking it. Lesson 10

Lesson 1 · The big idea Core · 2 min

Everything is one loop

Takeaway You say what done means; Claude runs the loop until it can prove it. Without a real test, it stops when it feels finished.

An AI agent is a loop: plan a step, do it, check the result (with a test, a command or an observation), and adjust. Orchestration, subagents (helpers that each take one job), hooks (scripts that run on their own) and schedules are all ways to run this loop better. A sharper goal (what you want done, and how you will know) makes the check honest. A better plan makes each step smaller. A stricter check stops the loop from ending early.

Running example (it comes back in later lessons). Take the goal "Users can export the reports table to CSV." Claude plans a small step and makes the change. Check then runs npm test: a fail sends it back to adjust, and only a pass lets it call the work done, with proof.

Three roles keep this loop healthy, and you will see them on every page of this guide:

  • You set the goal, the bar for done, and the moments Claude must stop and ask.
  • The lead session (the orchestrator) holds the plan and makes the calls.
  • Helpers and gates do side work and run checks the lead can't skip; a gate is a check that runs on its own.
What happens if Check is missing?

Claude stops when it feels finished, which is not the same as done. Why: the loop ends well only when Check is real, such as a test, a command or an observation.

Lesson 2 · Ten rules Reference · 4 min

Ten rules from the people who build it

Takeaway Give outcomes and a way to prove them, load only what the next step needs, and enforce must-happen rules in code.

These come from Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, from Andrej Karpathy, from Anthropic's engineering team, and from practitioners who run agents every day. Each source line carries a tag showing how solid it is. Hover over, focus or tap a tag to see its source; clicking P, S or R opens that source in a new tab. D tags are our own advice, so they only show the tooltip.

P their own words, or official docs S second-hand reports of a post R an independent research paper D advice built from the sources
  1. 01

    Keep the harness thin

    Let the model do the thinking. The harness is the scaffolding around it: tools, rules and checks. Every piece should name the failure it prevents, and go when a newer model no longer needs it.

    P Boris Cherny describes Claude Code as the thinnest possible wrapper over the model; better models absorb the scaffolding. Anthropic: start with the simplest thing that works.

  2. 02

    Make it prove its work

    A check Claude can run by itself is one of the biggest levers on quality.

    S Recaps of Boris Cherny's setup: a feedback loop improves results two to three times. P Anthropic's Agent SDK loop: gather context, act, verify, repeat.

  3. 03

    Give outcomes, not steps

    Say what done looks like and let Claude find the path.

    S Reports of Karpathy's notes: give success criteria and watch it go. P Anthropic: pitch prompts at the right altitude, then add rules only for failures you actually see.

  4. 04

    Treat context as a budget

    Load what the next step needs into the context window (Claude's working memory), not everything. Send heavy reading to helpers.

    S Karpathy endorsed "context engineering" over prompt engineering. P Anthropic: recall drops as the window fills; helpers return 1,000 to 2,000-token summaries.

  5. 05

    Let it search

    Fast grep-style search and a good map beat a retrieval pipeline for code.

    P Early Claude Code tried RAG with embeddings; plain agentic search outperformed it, by the team's own impressions rather than a benchmark.

  6. 06

    Plan before building

    Approve a plan of small, testable slices instead of approving every edit.

    S Boris Cherny starts most sessions in Plan mode; a good plan often lands in one shot. P Official best practices: explore, plan, code, commit.

  7. 07

    Keep maker and checker apart

    Reviewers get the work and the criteria, never the author's reasoning.

    P Best practices: an adversarial review subagent in a fresh context. Karpathy's llm-council has models review each other anonymously.

  8. 08

    Turn corrections into rules

    Capture each lesson, but keep CLAUDE.md short and push detail into skills and docs. A generated CLAUDE.md, such as /init output, added cost without helping in one study, so cut it to what Claude can't find out on its own. R D

    S Boris Cherny: after a correction, tell Claude to update CLAUDE.md. P Best practices: cut any CLAUDE.md line whose removal wouldn't cause a mistake.

  9. 09

    Enforce with code

    Anything that must happen every time lives in a hook (such as a Stop hook, which runs when Claude tries to finish), CI or a permission rule, not only in prose.

    P A Stop hook exiting with code 2 blocks Claude from finishing. Anthropic's long-running harness forbade editing tests and kept state in JSON.

  10. 10

    Spend compute where it pays

    Fan out for wide reading and judgment calls; stay single-agent for tightly coupled edits.

    P Anthropic's multi-agent research system beat a single agent by 90.2% on its internal eval, at about 15 times the tokens of a chat. Karpathy, October 2025: this is the decade of agents, and they're weak at truly new code. S By December he was doing most of his own coding through agents.

Lesson 3 · From idea to issues Builder · 4 min

From a business pain point to work an agent can finish

Takeaway By the end, every issue has an outcome, a runnable check and a boundary, and open questions are written down, not guessed.

Before Claude writes code, someone has to turn a vague pain into small issues that each carry a check. You own the why and the decision to spend time; the agent drafts, researches and asks.

Reference: what each stage produces (7 stages)
StageWhat it producesWho decidesMove on when
FrameThe job in the customer's words, and the number to moveYouThe outcome has a number
AssumptionsWhat must be true, ranked by importance and evidenceYou rank; the agent checks feasibility in the codeEach risky, unproven assumption has a test or a spike
GrillA decision log in the repoThe agent asks, you answer; it looks facts up itselfNothing is open, and you confirm the summary
ShapeA pitch: problem, time budget, sketch, rabbit holes, no-gosThe agent drafts; you set the time budgetRabbit holes resolved; no-gos written down
BetA project or cycle entryYouTime budget fixed; ideas you didn't bet on are parked
SpecifyStories with Given/When/Then, failure cases, open questionsThe agent drafts; you approveEvery criterion is observable; no guessed policy written as fact
SliceIssues with outcome, check, boundary and dependenciesThe agent drafts; you check the orderEach issue has a runnable check; a thin end-to-end slice comes first

D Our pipeline, built from these P sources: Jobs to Be Done, Teresa Torres' opportunity solution trees, assumption mapping, Basecamp's Shape Up (a time budget gives the agent a stop condition; no-gos become its scope fence), EARS failure-case requirements, Given/When/Then scenarios, INVEST and tracer bullets. S A common trap: AI-drafted specs state policy nobody agreed as fact, so keep an Open Questions section.

Running example. The pain: people want the reports table in a spreadsheet. Slice turns it into one issue: outcome "Users can export the reports table to CSV", boundary "code changes only in src/reports/, no new packages", and no dependencies. Its check has three lines: the export has exactly the rows on screen, npm test passes with a new test for an empty report, and the file opens in Excel with the same columns as the table.

Should you grill like Matt Pocock? Yes, with rules

Matt Pocock's grill-me skill runs a relentless interview that walks every branch of a design tree before any plan exists; he calls misalignment the top reason agent work fails. Harper Reed uses the same move before writing a spec, and Claude Code's own best practices say to have Claude interview you, then write a spec, then build in a fresh session. P

  • Grill anything bigger than a one-line fix.
  • One question per message, with Claude's recommended answer and its cost. Pocock's own versions differ: one asks a question at a time, the newer one asks in rounds. Rounds get skimmed. His current skill words each question so a plain "yes" accepts the recommendation.
  • Claude never asks you a fact it can look up in the code, docs or data.
  • Keep the decision log in a file in the repo.
  • Stop when nothing is open, then confirm Claude's summary.
  • Write the spec in a fresh session, from the log.
  • Pocock's own caveat: no spec catches everything, so keep a QA loop that turns findings into new issues. P
Reference: how much spec before code

Small fix

An issue with a check.

Normal feature

A grill log, a one-page spec with Given/When/Then and open questions, then sliced issues.

Large or risky

Add a research doc and a decision record, an adversarial review, and your sign-off.

P Birgitta Böckeler (martinfowler.com) found generated output varies between regenerations. D So treat the spec as intent, and keep the tests as the real contract.

Lesson 4 · Goals Core · 3 min

Write a goal Claude can check

Takeaway State the result you want and two to five checks that prove it, plus when Claude must stop and ask.

Claude is very good at doing. It needs you to define done. A goal without a test is a wish. Good goals have five parts:

  • OutcomeWhat is true when it's finished. Describe the result, not the activity.
  • Done when2 to 5 checks a command or a person can run. These are your success criteria.
  • ConstraintsWhat's off limits: files, packages, style, spending.
  • Stop and ask ifThe moments Claude must hand control back to you.
  • BudgetHow much effort: one session, how many helpers, which model.

Weak goal

"Make the reports page better."

Better how? Claude will guess, polish things you didn't ask for, and call it done when it runs out of ideas.

Strong goal

Outcome
Users can export the reports table to CSV.
Done when
1. Export downloads exactly the rows on screen. 2. npm test passes, with a new test for an empty report. 3. The file opens in Excel with the same columns as the table.
Constraints
Only change code in src/reports/; plans and notes go in docs/. No new packages.
Stop and ask if
A database change looks needed, or the same test fails twice.
Budget
One session, up to 3 helper agents.
In the CSV goal, "up to 3 helper agents" belongs under which of the five parts, and "No new packages" under which?

Budget, then Constraints. Why: Budget is how much effort to spend; Constraints is what is off limits, such as files and packages.

Build your goal prompt

Fill in the fields. The box on the right turns them into a full orchestration prompt you can paste into Claude. It starts filled with the example above.

One check per line.
One per line.
One per line. "Anything hard to undo" is always added.
Effort and stop limits. Repeating and scheduled runs always need a cap.
Used by scheduled runs. Cloud runs start from a fresh copy each time, so files don't carry over.
Paste the prompt and press Enter.

Your prompt


    

  

  
Try now (10 min)

  
    
    
  1. Pick a small task of your own that you can check in a minute or two.
    2. 
    
  2. Write a goal with the five parts: Outcome, Done when (2 to 5 checks), Constraints, Stop and ask if, Budget. The builder above can help.
    3. 
    
  3. Paste it into Claude and add: "At the end, give me a receipt: each Done when line marked PASS, FAIL or NOT RUN, with the command behind it."
    4. 
    
  4. Let Claude work. If it reaches a Stop and ask if line, answer it.
    5. 
    
  5. Read the receipt. You are done when every line shows PASS with its command; FAIL or NOT RUN means it is not done, so paste the receipt back and name the line to fix.
    6.

Lesson 5 · Phases Core · 3 min

  
The ten phases, in four stages

  
Takeaway Ten phases take big tasks from goal to ship. Critique and Learn get skipped, but matter most when Claude works alone.

  
Big tasks pass through the same phases. Small tasks skip some: a typo fix is just Frame, Build, Verify. The orange arrows are the loops back, where a phase sends work to an earlier one. Frame is the short version of Lesson 3: for a new idea, run the full discovery first. Select a phase to see what happens in it.


  

  
Two phases are the ones people skip, and they matter most for letting the agent work on its own:

  
    
    
  • Critique (advisory review) happens before building. A fresh reviewer that never saw Claude's reasoning argues against the plan. As HumanLayer puts it, a bad line in a plan costs more than a bad line of code.
    • 
    
  • Learn turns each run into better rules for the next one. Without it, you correct the same mistakes forever.
    • 
  

  
When a task needs knowledge Claude lacks, Explore searches in order: this repo first, then the official docs, then other projects for ideas, not code to paste. Check that every new dependency really exists in its registry, since models invent package names, then pin it. Copy code only under a permissive licence, and note where it came from. R D

  
Running example. For the CSV export, Explore returns a few short reports with file paths: where the reports table gets its rows and its columns. Plan is a plan file in docs/ with ordered slices, the test for each, and how to undo each one. Verify ends in a receipt: PASS, FAIL or NOT RUN, with the command, for each of the three Done when lines.

  
Which of the ten phases comes before anything is built and has a fresh reviewer argue against the plan?
Critique. Why: a reviewer that never saw Claude's reasoning argues against the plan before building starts.

Lesson 6 · Orchestration Core · 5 min

  
One lead, many helpers

  
Takeaway Send helpers wide reading, parallel jobs and fresh-eyes review. Keep small jobs, and jobs that touch the same files, in the lead.

  
Orchestration means one Claude session acts as the lead. It holds the goal, the plan and the decisions. It hands narrow jobs to helper agents (subagents). Each helper starts with a clean memory, does one job (a builder works in its own worktree, a separate copy of the project's code), and sends back a short summary. The lead sees the conclusion, not the pile of reading behind it, and ends by giving you a receipt: each success criterion marked PASS, FAIL or NOT RUN, with the command behind it.


  

  
Why helpers keep the lead sharp

  
Every file Claude reads fills its context window, its working memory. When the window gets full, older turns are compressed and early details fade. Helpers do their reading in their own windows, so the lead stays light.


  

  
Running example. The CSV goal allows up to 3 helpers, so the lead sends a scout to read how the table builds its rows and columns, a builder to make the export in its own worktree, and a verifier to re-run the checks. Before and after, with made-up numbers (illustrative, not measured): one session reading everything itself opens about 40 files and its window fills with raw reading; with the scout, the lead receives 3 short summaries. The lead keeps the plan and the final say on "done".


  

    Reality check
    
One writer by default. Fan out only for parallel, read-heavy work; steps that depend on each other go worse with more agents. External checks beat self-critique. See Lesson 17.

  


  

    

      
Send a helper when

      
    
        
  • The reading is wide (many files, many pages) and you only need the conclusion.
    • 
        
  • Jobs don't depend on each other, so they can run at the same time.
    • 
        
  • You want a judgment from someone who didn't do the work: review, critique.
    • 
        
  • A cheaper model can do it: search, summarize, list.
    • 
      

    

    

      
Do it in the lead when

      
    
        
  • It's a handful of steps and you know where to look.
    • 
        
  • The next step needs every detail, not a summary.
    • 
        
  • Writing the brief would take longer than doing the job.
    • 
        
  • Two helpers would edit the same files.
    • 
      

    

  


  
Sort these 6 jobs into lead or helper: (a) read many files and report only the conclusion; (b) change one line in a file you already have open; (c) fix a failing test from the exact error text you just saw; (d) review a finished change you did not write; (e) list every place a name appears; (f) two jobs that would both edit the same file.
Helper: a, d, e. Lead: b, c, f. Why: a is wide reading where only the conclusion matters, d needs a judge who didn't do the work, e is a cheap list job; b would take longer to brief than to do, c needs every detail, f would have two helpers editing the same file.


  
Brief a helper like a capable colleague who knows nothing yet. Its brief is the only context it gets. Say the goal, what's already ruled out, where to look, the scope, and the exact format to return. When you ask for a review, hand over the code and the criteria, not your conclusion. A reviewer that reads your conclusion tends to agree with it.

Lesson 7 · Patterns and methods Builder · 5 min

  
Pick the right shape for the job

  
Takeaway Plan, critique, build is the default for most coding. Use a specialist pattern only when your task matches its “Use it when” column.

  
Most work needs one agent with a plan, a critic and good checks. Reach for the bigger shapes only when the task has the property they're built for.


  

    

      
PatternHow it worksUse it whenWatch out for

Goal loop P/goal: an evaluator re-checks after each turn until your condition holdsOne session with a provable end stateThe condition must show in the output

        
Lead + workers PThe lead splits work as it goes; workers report back summariesWide reading and researchAbout 15 times chat tokens

        
Specialist: use when the task fits

        
Prompt chain PFixed steps with a check between eachThe stages are known in advanceBrittle when a stage varies

        
Parallel sections PIndependent parts run at onceParts don't depend on each otherTwo writers on one file

        
Evaluator + optimizer PGenerate, critique, reviseThe criteria are clearEndless loops when they aren't

        
Initializer + worker PSession one writes a feature list (JSON, all failing) and a progress file; each later session finishes one featureProjects that span many sessionsDeclaring victory early

        
Ralph loop PA shell loop feeds the same prompt to a fresh agent; state lives on disk; one item per passA well-specified backlog with strong testsNo cap: one user's plugin loop ran 6,239 times (GitHub issue)

        
Hill-climbing PTry a change for a fixed few minutes; keep it if one metric improves, git reset if not; repeat until stoppedOne cheap, trustworthy metricGaming the metric; the repo only tells the agent not to touch the evaluation, so lock it for real

        
Council PSeveral models answer, rank each other anonymously, a chair writes the verdictJudgment calls with no testAbout 9 model calls by default; a vibe-coded Saturday hack, unsupported

        
Day shift, night shift PYou grill and plan by day; a sandboxed loop (its shell commands run in a restricted space) builds the issues overnight; QA findings become new issuesA backlog of well-sliced issuesNeeds a real sandbox

Lesson 8 · Toolbox Builder · 4 min

  
Which Claude feature does which job

  
Takeaway Start with five features: CLAUDE.md for standing rules, Plan mode, Skills, Subagents and Hooks. Look up the rest when a job needs them.

  
Each piece of the loop has a feature built for it. Most of the skill in orchestration is picking the right one.


  

    

      
JobFeatureIn plain wordsReach for it when

      
        
Start with these five

        
Standing rulesCLAUDE.mdA rulebook Claude reads at the start of every session.Something should be true every time: "use pnpm", "never touch prod".

Repeat a recipeSkillsA saved procedure, run as /name or loaded when the task matches.You've explained the same process twice.

        
Side jobsSubagentsHelpers with a clean context, their own tools and model. They return a summary.Wide reading, parallel work, fresh-eyes review.

        
Checks it can't skipHooksYour own scripts that run on events, like re-running tests when Claude tries to stop.A check must happen every single time.

        
Reach for these when a job needs them

        
Big fan-outsDynamic workflowsClaude writes a script that runs dozens to hundreds of helpers. Their results stay out of the main context, and verifier agents cross-check claims. Start with /workflows or /deep-research.Large audits, research, migrations. Uses many tokens.

        
Many PRs at once/batchSplits a change across 5 to 30 helpers, each in its own worktree, each opening a PR.Mechanical changes across many files.

        
Repeat now/loopRe-runs a prompt in this session every N minutes, or at a pace Claude picks. Stops with the session; repeating tasks expire after 7 days.Watching a deploy, polling a queue, chipping at a backlog.

Remote Control lets your phone drive a session on your laptop.Laptop closed, or checking in from your phone.

    Example: one author's harness (other setups differ)
    
One person's Claude setup, shown as an example: it has a helper for most phases. Here is where each one fits:

    

      
Discovery
A kickoff skill and a shaping skill; a grilling skill that asks one question per message.

      
Explore
The Explore agent and Haiku scouts for reading sweeps; doc-checker to test a claim against the real docs.

      
Plan
Plan mode, the planner agent (plans and ADR drafts), the writing-plans skill.

      
Critique
adversarial-reviewer returns up to three blocking objections, or none; a second-model review gives another view.

      
Review
audit-reader, /code-review, a diff reviewer agent.

      
Verify
A Stop gate and a pre-push chain rerun the checks; release-verifier for a check no gate runs.

      
How much
Review tiers. T0: run the tests once. T1: the gates. T2: the full process with the adversary.

Lesson 9 · Self-checks Core · 3 min

  
Make Claude prove its own work

  
Takeaway The builder never grades its own work. Ask for a receipt: each criterion marked PASS, FAIL or NOT RUN, with its command.

  
A success criterion only helps if something checks it. Turn each criterion into a test scenario, then into a gate that runs whether or not anyone remembers.


  
    
    
  1. 
      Step 1
      
    Criterion
    
      
    What must be true, in words.
    
      
    Export downloads exactly the rows on screen.
    
    
    2. 
    
  2. 
      Step 2
      
    Scenario
    
      
    A concrete case: given, when, then.
    
      
    Given 3 rows filtered to 2, when I click Export, then the CSV has a header and 2 rows.
    
    
    3. 
    
  3. 
      Step 3
      
    Gate
    
      
    Something that runs it every time.
    
      
    A test in npm test, rerun by a Stop hook (a script that runs when Claude tries to finish) and by CI on every push.
    
    
    4. 
  


  
Scenarios to ask for every time

  
    
    
  • Happy path: normal use works.
    • 
    
  • Edge cases: empty, huge, odd characters, the first and last item.
    • 
    
  • Bad input: wrong type, missing field, no permission.
    • 
    
  • Regression: the thing that broke last time still works.
    • 
    
  • Failure: the network is down or a service times out, and the error is clear.
    • 
  


  

    Golden rule
    
The builder never grades its own homework. The check comes from a command, a hook, or a fresh agent.

  


  
Read-only tests aren't enough. Where the tests contradicted the spec, models passed by editing the tests or by special-casing them, and making the tests read-only stopped only the edits. R Keep one acceptance check outside Claude's workspace, run by CI or the Stop hook, and let Claude report that a task can't be done as written. D

  
If an LLM judge scores the work, use a model from a different family, or an execution check, and run it more than once: a judge favours its own outputs R and may not agree with itself from one run to the next. R D

  
The trust ladder

  
Each rung catches more, and costs more. Climb as high as the risk calls for: a typo fix needs rung 2; a change to login, payments or the database needs rungs 5 and 6.

  
Who checksWhat it catchesTrust

  
    
    
  1. 1 · Claude says it's doneNothing on its own. A claim, not a check.
    2. 
    
  2. 2 · Claude shows the command and output enough for a typo fixObvious failures, typos, broken builds.
    3. 
    
  3. 3 · A hook reruns the checksSkipped steps and checks that were never run.
    4. 
    
  4. 4 · A fresh agent reviews the changeThe builder's blind spots, weakened tests.
    5. 
    
  5. 5 · An adversary tries to break it login, payments, dataDesign flaws, security holes, bad edge cases.
    6. 
    
  6. 6 · You sign off login, payments, dataA wrong goal. Only you know what you meant.
    7. 
  


  
Ask for a receipt at the end of every task: each criterion with PASS, FAIL or NOT RUN, and the command behind it. A receipt makes "done" something you can check in ten seconds.

  
75% per run: what's the chance 3 runs in a row all pass?
About 42% (0.75 × 0.75 × 0.75 ≈ 0.42). Why: for unattended work, what counts is how often every run succeeds, not whether one did.

  
For anything that runs unattended, measure how often every run succeeds, not whether one did. At 75% success per run, three runs in a row all succeed only about 42% of the time. Anthropic's eval guidance calls this pass^k. P

Lesson 10 · Guardrails Builder · 4 min

  
Guardrails that hold when nobody is watching

  
Takeaway Deny rules win in every mode. Never give one session all three: private data, untrusted content, a way to send data out.

  

    
Start with these 3

    
    
      
  1. Deny rules for secrets. A deny always beats an allow, in every mode. P
    2. 
      
  2. Sandbox on, with no unsandboxed retries. It covers shell commands only. P
    3. 
      
  3. In every session, remove one of the three dangers in the figure below: private data, untrusted content, or a way to send data out. P
    4. 
    

    
Good enough for a solo developer: these three are enough to start. The rest of this lesson is for teams and unattended runs. D

  

  
An instruction in a prompt is a request. Guardrails that hold live at the level of tools, the operating system and accounts, where the agent can't talk its way past them.


  



  

    Reference: 6 facts to design around
  
    
    
  • Deny rules win. Claude Code checks deny, then ask, then allow; an allow can't override a deny, and deny rules hold in every mode. P
    • 
    
  • Auto mode is a convenience, not a wall. One independent stress test, using deliberately ambiguous tasks, found it missed 81% of risky actions. Anthropic's own 17% miss rate comes from a small curated set, not from live traffic. R
    • 
    
  • The sandbox only covers shell commands. File reads and edits, web fetches, MCP servers and hooks run outside it. Anthropic reports 84% fewer permission prompts with it on. Claude can also retry a failed command outside the sandbox; set allowUnsandboxedCommands: false to stop that. P
    • 
    
  • Managed settings beat repo settings, but only if you have a managed policy. With allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly on, repo allow, ask and deny rules are all ignored, so keep your deny rules in the managed file. Without a policy, run agents only in checkouts you trust. P
    • 
    
  • Headless runs (Claude called from a script, with no chat window) trust the repo. claude -p without --bare runs the repo's hooks and MCP servers with no prompt. With --bare your own hooks don't run either, so put the checks in the CI job. P
    • 
    
  • Skills and tools are code you didn't write. A scan of 98,380 community skills confirmed 157 malicious ones, and poisoned MCP tool descriptions reached 72.8% attack success against the most vulnerable agent tested. R
    • 
  

  

  

    Reference: 17 controls to prevent, detect and recover
  

    

      
Prevent

      
    
        
  • Deny rules for secrets, enforced through managed settings
    • 
        
  • Sandbox on, with no unsandboxed retries; block reads of SSH and cloud keys with both sandbox and Read deny rules; a tiny network allowlist
    • 
        
  • No blanket shell allows when using auto mode
    • 
        
  • Drop one trifecta leg per session
    • 
        
  • Read and pin skills, plugins and MCP servers
    • 
        
  • Short-lived, narrowly scoped tokens
    • 
      

    

    

      
Detect

      
    
        
  • Log every tool call with a PreToolUse hook
    • 
        
  • Alert on denials and repeated blocks
    • 
        
  • Alert on edits to settings, CLAUDE.md, hooks and skills
    • 
        
  • Log network traffic leaving the sandbox
    • 
        
  • OpenTelemetry for sessions and cost
    • 
        
  • A StopFailure hook, so API errors and rate limits don't end a run silently
    • 
        
  • Logs the agent can't edit, with secrets redacted
    • 
      

    

    

      
Recover

      
    
        
  • Commit, or use a worktree, before long runs
    • 
        
  • Snapshot memory and rule files
    • 
        
  • Your approval, shown as a dry-run diff, for delete, send, publish, deploy and pay
    • 
        
  • A written kill switch: disable the task, stop the session, revoke its tokens, revert its branch
    • 
      

    

  

  

  

    Reference: 7 top mistakes
  
    
    
  • Treating auto mode, or any "95% detection" filter, as a security boundary.
    • 
    
  • Skipping permission checks in a container that has your credentials mounted.
    • 
    
  • Blanket allows for the shell or script interpreters.
    • 
    
  • Assuming the sandbox covers file reads, hooks or MCP servers.
    • 
    
  • Letting a repo's own settings grant permissions, with no managed policy above them.
    • 
    
  • Installing community skills and MCP servers without reading them.
    • 
    
  • Loops with no cap on iterations, time or cost.
    • 
  

  

  
More in the playbook: §10Next: 11 Running nonstop →↑ Contents







  
Lesson 11 · Running nonstop Builder · 4 min

  
Keep it running without you

  
Takeaway Any run without you needs a stop condition, a retry cap, a cost ceiling and a home for its results.

  
There are three ways to make Claude work continuously. They differ in what wakes it up and whether your computer has to stay on.


  

  
Guardrails for anything that runs without you

  
    
    
  • A stop condition"Stop when every check passes, or after 10 runs." No open-ended loops.
    • 
    
  • A retry capAfter 2 failures with the same cause, stop and report. Don't try a third time.
    • 
    
  • Safe to repeatRunning twice must not send twice, charge twice, or create duplicates.
    • 
    
  • Short reportsOne line per run, and "no change" when nothing happened.
    • 
    
  • A home for resultsA file, a ticket, or a message. Not just the chat history.
    • 
    
  • Tight permissionsAllow only the tools it needs. Deleting, deploying, pushing to main and paying wait for you; pushing to its own branch is fine.
    • 
    
  • A cost ceilingPick the model and the interval on purpose. Every 5 minutes adds up fast.
    • 
    
  • Fresh context each passStart each run clean and read state from files, or compact on purpose. A context that runs for hours drifts.
    • 
  


  
Terminal, cloud, phone

  
Where each part of the work happens once you stop sitting at the screen.

  

    

      
Terminal

      
Runs
Interactive sessions, plan mode, /loop, desktop scheduled tasks.

      
You do
Write the brief, grill, approve the plan, push the branch before handing off.

      
Limit
The machine has to stay awake.

    

    

      
Cloud

      
Runs
claude --cloud sessions, scheduled tasks, @claude in GitHub, auto-fix on PRs, Linear coding sessions.

      
You do
Pick the environment and network level, queue tasks, review PRs.

      
Limit
Works from your GitHub repo or an uploaded copy; you open the PR. Idle VMs get reclaimed, so state must live in git and files.

    

    

      
Phone

      
Runs
The Claude app or claude.ai/code; Remote Control into your laptop's session.

      
You do
Triage, answer questions, nudge, start cloud tasks.

      
Limit
Remote Control needs the laptop awake. Review real diffs on a big screen.

    

  

  
    
    
  • Cloud sessions keep running after you close the laptop, and count against your plan limits. P
    • 
    
  • Teleport pulls a cloud branch into your terminal, one way; after that the two copies drift apart. P
    • 
    
  • Auto-fix answers CI failures and review comments under your GitHub account, so it can set off comment-driven deploy bots. P
    • 
    
  • Use --max-budget-usd on headless runs; /usage is a local estimate and the Console is the real bill. P
    • 
    
  • A scheduled task can pause to ask you something, so check for paused runs as well as failed ones. Each run starts from a fresh clone and pushes to a claude/ branch, so keep its state in a ticket or PR comment, not in files. P
    • 
    
  • We found no per-session dollar cap for cloud sessions as of October 2026. D
    • 
    
  • Every background agent (Codex, Cursor, Jules, Devin, GitHub Copilot) lands on the same shape: fresh VM, branch, pull request. They differ in network access and where you start them. S
    • 
  

  
More in the playbook: §11Next: 12 Linear + GitHub →↑ Contents







  
Lesson 12 · Linear and GitHub Builder · 4 min

  
From ticket to merged PR without watching

  
Takeaway You act at the edges: write the issue, delegate, approve. Protect the gate files so the agent can't switch off its own checks.

  
The shape that works: Linear holds intent and status, the agent works in a sandbox, GitHub holds the code and the gates, and you approve at the edges.


  

  
Running example. The CSV issue from Lesson 3 goes into Triage, and you delegate it. The agent opens a branch and a draft PR, and the required checks run npm test, including the empty-report test. Your team's GitHub automation moves the issue to In Review; after you approve, merging the PR that says "Fixes ID" moves it to Done.


  

      
Who moves each status

      
    
        
  • Triage to Todo (steps 1–2): you, or a triage rule.
    • 
        
  • Todo to In Progress (steps 2–4): the agent, when you delegate.
    • 
        
  • In Progress to In Review (step 9): your team's GitHub automation (check its settings), not the agent.
    • 
        
  • In Review to Done (steps 10–12): merging a PR that says "Fixes ID", after your approval.
    • 
        
  • Anything to awaiting input (step 8): the agent, with a question instead of a guess.
    • 
      

  



  

    Reference: the gate at each step (6)
      
    
        
  • Intake (steps 1–2): only people with write access can trigger the agent; bots allowed by name.
    • 
        
  • Agent run (steps 3–5, 7–8): its own branch prefix and pushes only there, a read-only token otherwise, only the tools it needs, no secrets, a network allowlist.
    • 
        
  • Draft PR (step 5): the agent can't approve or merge.
    • 
        
  • Checks (steps 6–7): required checks in a ruleset; a person approves workflow runs on agent PRs.
    • 
        
  • Review (step 10): AI comments only; a person approves, and not the one who asked.
    • 
        
  • Merge and deploy (steps 11–12): merge queue reruns checks; environment reviewers, no admin bypass.
    • 
      

  

  

    Reference: 7 things worth knowing about GitHub and Linear
  
    
    
  • Set up the Claude GitHub Action with /install-github-app; trigger it with @claude, a label or assignment. Bots are blocked by default, but any bot you allow-list skips the permission check, so never allow every bot on a public repo. P
    • 
    
  • On PR runs the action restores .claude/, CLAUDE.md and .mcp.json from the base branch, but package scripts still come from the PR. P
    • 
    
  • pull_request_target runs with secrets: never check out and run PR code there. Pass issue and PR text through env:, and pin actions to a full commit SHA. P
    • 
    
  • CODEOWNERS is read from the base branch, so a PR can't add its own owners. A merge queue needs CI to listen for merge_group. P
    • 
    
  • In Linear you stay the assignee and the agent is a delegate. Put repo and gate rules in Linear's agent guidance once, not in every ticket; it's advice to the agent, not a gate. P
    • 
    
  • Approving every step wears you down: users accept 93% of Claude Code's permission prompts, and Anthropic warns that over time this leads to approval fatigue. P
    • 
    
  • A high merge rate doesn't mean good PRs: who submits a PR predicts its merge more than what it changes. Track reverts and bugs found after shipping instead. R D
    • 
    
  • Link work with "Fixes ID" in the PR; commit magic words can close an issue without any review. P
    • 
    
  • Field report: small, specific tickets merged cleanly, while a vague "make it snappier" ticket got a cosmetic fix that missed the real cause. S
    • 
  

  


  

    Protect the gates
    
An agent that can edit CI, hooks or gate config can switch off its own checks. Put those files behind path rules and code-owner review.

Lesson 13 · Growing Builder · 3 min

  
Plan, measure, improve

  
Takeaway After ten tasks, the trend in your scorecard shows where to invest. Growing also means pruning rules that never fire.

  
An agent setup gets better only if each run teaches the next one. That takes a short retro after real work, and a few numbers to tell you whether it's working.


  

  

    

      
Signs you are planning

      
    
        
  • A plan file exists before the first edit.
    • 
        
  • Every slice names the test that proves it.
    • 
        
  • Risks and the way to undo each change are written down.
    • 
        
  • Big decisions are recorded with the reason (an ADR or a short note).
    • 
        
  • When reality changes, the plan changes, and the change is noted.
    • 
      

    

    

      
Signs you are growing

      
    
        
  • Verify passes on the first try more often.
    • 
        
  • You step in to correct Claude less often.
    • 
        
  • Fewer bugs turn up after shipping.
    • 
        
  • Your CLAUDE.md and skills change a little every week, and stay short.
    • 
        
  • Tasks you used to watch now run on /loop or /schedule.
    • 
      

    

  


  
A scorecard to track per task

  
Keep it in a simple log: one row per real task. After ten rows the trend tells you where to invest.

  

    

      
MeasureHow to count itWhat it tells youWant

      
        
First-try passDid Verify pass without going back to Build?Plan and criteria quality.↑ Up

        
Rework loopsTimes work bounced from Verify or Review back to Build.Where checks are catching late what planning should catch early.↓ Down

        
Your correctionsTimes you had to step in or redirect.Missing rules, vague goals, missing stop conditions.↓ Down

        
Escaped bugsProblems found after shipping.Missing scenarios or gates.↓ Down

        
Cost per taskTokens or minutes, from OpenTelemetry or the Console bill.Over-delegation or loops that run too often.→ Steady

        
All-runs pass rateRun the same task k times: did every run pass?Whether unattended loops are reliable or just lucky.↑ Up

      
    

  

  
Keep a rule or skill mined from past sessions only if re-running your eval set shows it helps. Without a reliable signal of what worked, lessons a model writes for itself can leave it worse off. R D

  
Running example. The CSV row in the log shows one rework loop: Verify sent the work back to Build once, because the first file held a row the filter had hidden. The retro picks one change: turn the check "3 rows filtered to 2" into a test in npm test, so the gate catches it on the next run.

  
More in the playbook: §13Next: 14 Prompt library →↑ Contents







  
Lesson 14 · Prompt library Reference · 6 min

  
Prompts that make Claude work on its own

  
Takeaway Pick the template for the step you're on; paste Self-check before Claude wraps up and Retro after a real task.

  
Copy one, fill in the parts in angle brackets, and paste it into Claude. The goal prompt from Lesson 4 is the main one; these cover the rest of the loop.


  

    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
  


  

    
Claude researches on its own, merges what it found, recommends, and has its pick challenged before you see it.


Research question: <the question>
It feeds this decision: <what I will decide with the answer>

1. Explore. Start 3 read-only helper agents in parallel, one per angle:
   a) <angle 1, e.g. official docs>
   b) <angle 2, e.g. our codebase>
   c) <angle 3, e.g. known problems and bug reports>
   Each returns up to 10 findings, each with a source (file:line or link)
   and a confidence: high, medium or low.
2. Synthesize. Merge them into one brief: what the sources agree on,
   where they conflict, and what is still unknown. Every claim keeps its source.
3. Recommend. Give 2 or 3 options with trade-offs, then your pick and why.
4. Advisory review. Send only the brief, not your reasoning, to a fresh
   reviewer agent. Tell it to argue against your pick and name its
   blocking objections, up to 3, or say there are none.
5. Answer each objection: change the pick, or explain why it stands.
6. Save the final brief to docs/research/<topic>.md and show me
   a 5-line summary.

  


  

    
Paste before Claude wraps up. It turns "done" into a receipt you can check.


Before you tell me this is done:

1. List every success criterion from the goal.
2. For each one, run the check. Show the command and the last lines
   of its output.
3. Mark each PASS, FAIL or NOT RUN (say why). NOT RUN is not PASS.
4. Also test these scenarios:
   - Happy path: <normal use>
   - Edge case: <empty, huge or unusual input>
   - Bad input: <wrong type, missing field>
   - Regression: <the thing that broke last time>
5. Start a fresh reviewer agent. Give it only the diff and the criteria,
   not your summary. Fix or answer each finding.
6. Then write the summary: what changed, what passed, what is not done.

  


  

    
The shape of a good brief for any helper agent. Use it yourself, or tell the lead to brief helpers this way.


Goal: <what you need back, and the decision it feeds>
Already ruled out: <what has been checked, so it is not redone>
Look here: <files, folders, URLs>
Scope: read-only. Do not edit anything. Stop after <N> files or sources.
Return: up to 10 findings, each with a file:line or link and a
confidence (high, medium, low). Say plainly what you could not find.

  


  

    
Repeats inside this session while it stays open. Leave out "30m" to let Claude choose its own pace.


/loop 30m Check <what to watch, e.g. the deploy, the open PRs, the failing tests>.
If <condition>, do <one small action> and report it in one line.
If nothing changed, reply "no change" and nothing else.
Never <the thing it must not do>; ask me instead.
Stop the loop when <end condition>, or after 2 failures with the same cause.

  


  

    
Sets up a cloud scheduled task that runs on a timetable, even with your computer off. It can still pause to ask you something. Describe the timing in plain words.


/schedule Every weekday at 8:00:
<the task, e.g. read yesterday's failed CI runs and group them by cause>.
Write the result to <where: a file, a ticket, a message>.
Keep it under 15 lines, most important first.
If something fails, say what failed and stop. Try again at most once.
Never <push, delete, or contact anyone>; leave a note for me instead.

  


  

    
Two minutes after a real task. This is the Learn phase, and how the setup grows.


Retro on this task. Be specific and short.

1. Where did we spend more turns than we should have, and why?
2. What did I have to correct you on?
3. Which check caught a real problem? Which check was missing?
4. Did any helper agent waste effort or come back empty?
   What was wrong with its brief?
5. Propose up to 3 changes that would make the next run better.
   Each is a CLAUDE.md rule, a skill, a hook or a test.
   Show the exact text or code.
Don't apply anything until I say yes.

  


  

    
Discovery before any plan: Claude interviews you until the design is settled, and writes nothing else.


Grill me about <idea>. The goal is shared understanding before any plan or spec.
Rules:
- One question per message. Give your recommended answer and what it costs.
- Never ask me something you can find in the code, docs or data.
  Look it up and tell me what you found.
- Walk the design tree: settle prerequisite questions before the ones
  that depend on them.
- Keep a decision log in docs/discovery/<topic>.md: question, answer, reason.
- Cover: who struggles and when, the outcome metric, the time budget,
  no-gos, rabbit holes, failure cases, open questions.
- Stop when nothing is open or after <N> questions, then summarize
  the decisions for me to confirm.
Do not write a plan, spec or code in this session.

  


  

    
The shape of an issue an agent can finish on its own, in Linear or GitHub.


Title: <verb> <thing>
Outcome: <the observable result when this is done>
Today: <what happens now, with steps to reproduce if it's a bug>
Where: <files or functions, if known>
Check: <the command or Given/When/Then scenario that proves it's done>
Boundary: <in scope> / No-gos: <out of scope>
Depends on: <issue IDs, or none>
Open questions: <none, or a list; the agent asks instead of guessing>
Risk: <trivial | normal | high>

Lesson 15 · When it goes wrong Core · 3 min

  
Common failures and their fixes

  
Takeaway Match the symptom to its likely cause, then apply the fix. After two failures with the same cause, stop and get a second opinion.

  
Almost every problem with autonomous agents traces back to a missing goal, a missing check, too much in one context, or too much permission.

  
Claude keeps retrying the CSV export test and has failed with the same error five times. What is the likely cause?
No retry cap. Why: the fix is a rule to stop after 2 failures with the same cause and ask a fresh agent for a second opinion, like the "same test fails twice" line in the Lesson 4 goal.


  

    

      
CauseWhat you seeLikely causeFix

      
        
goalWanders, gold-platesThe goal has no "done when".Add checkable criteria and a stop rule.

        
check"Done!" but brokenThe builder graded its own work.Require command output; add a hook or a fresh verifier.

        
contextForgets early detailsThe lead's context filled up with raw reading.Send reading to helpers; keep the plan in a file.

        
goalSame error, fifth tryNo retry cap.Stop after 2 failures with the same cause; ask a fresh agent for a second opinion.

        
checkReviewer always agreesIt read your reasoning first.Give it only the code and criteria; ask it to argue against.

        
goalHuge token billHelpers spawned for small jobs, or a loop that runs too often.Delegate only wide reading, parallel work or fresh judgment; slow the loop.

        
permissionsAgents overwrite each otherTwo writers on the same files.One writer per set of files; use worktrees.

        
permissionsOvernight run did something riskyToo much permission.Allow-list its tools; keep irreversible actions behind your approval.

        
permissionsAuto mode let something throughIt was treated as a security boundary.Rely on deny rules, the sandbox and managed settings; auto mode is a convenience.

        
goalThe loop ran all nightNo cap on iterations, time or cost.Cap all three. One uncapped loop ran 6,239 iterations.

        
checkTests pass, spec still brokenThe loop optimized for the tests it had.Keep a fresh-eyes review even when everything is green.

        
permissionsAgent turned off its own checksIt could edit CI, hook or gate files.Path rules and code-owner review on those files.

        
permissionsCI ran the repo's hooks unexpectedlyclaude -p without --bare.Use --bare (then run your checks as CI steps), or run only on a trusted checkout.

        
checkRun ended with no receiptAn API error or rate limit; the Stop gate never ran.Add a StopFailure hook that records the failure and notifies you.

      
    

  

  
Running example. The CSV builder said "Done!", but the file had 3 rows when the screen showed 2: it included the row the filter had hidden. That is the "Done!" but broken row: the builder graded its own work, so nobody ran the check. The fix was a fresh verifier running "Given 3 rows filtered to 2…" and recording FAIL; the work went back to Build, and the receipt now shows PASS with the command.

Lesson 17 · What the evidence says Reference · 6 min

  
Proven orchestration, by the evidence

  
Takeaway The evidence backs one writer by default, outside checks over self-critique, and measuring repeated runs and cost, not single wins.

  
This lesson counts only measured results: peer-reviewed or well-cited studies, research reports, and engineering write-ups from large teams that publish numbers. No YouTube and no product marketing. When a company reports on its own product, the playbook marks it as vendor-reported.


  

  
Six findings that hold up

  
    
    
  1. 01
    One writer by default
    Fan out only for parallel, read-heavy work. Steps that depend on each other go worse with more agents.
    Anthropic's 2026 guidance: start with one agent and split by context boundary, not job title. P Thoughtworks puts coding-agent swarms on caution. P
    2. 
    
  2. 02
    Wrap the model in a scripted pipeline
    At scale, teams script targeting, checks and merging, and call the model only for the edit.
    Airbnb finished a test migration estimated at 1.5 engineer-years in about 6 weeks. P
    More numbers
    Airbnb's run covered about 3,500 test files: 75% done in 4 hours and 97% in four days. Google: 74% of 595 migration changes were model-generated, then validated and sent to code owners for review. R Spotify has merged 1,500+ agent PRs behind build and test checks and a stop hook. P
    3. 
    
  3. 03
    External checks beat self-critique
    Tests, builds and a verifier step raise reliability; asking a model to re-check itself without a signal doesn't.
    Adding a verifier raised success by 15.6 points in one multi-agent framework. R Self-correction without outside feedback lowered reasoning accuracy. R
    More numbers
    The verifier result comes from 1,600+ traces. Meta kept only generated tests that built, passed and added coverage; engineers accepted 73% of those. R
    4. 
    
  4. 04
    Design the tools, keep the shape simple
    A better agent-computer interface or a fixed pipeline often beats a complex agent.
    SWE-agent's purpose-built file tools added 10.7 points over a raw shell. R
    More numbers
    A fixed localize-repair-validate pipeline solved 32% of SWE-bench Lite at about $0.70 per issue. R A simple retry baseline scored 93.2% for $2.45 where a complex agent scored 88.0% for $134.50. R
    5. 
    
  5. 05
    Measure reliability and cost
    One good run flatters an agent; repeated runs and full test suites tell the truth.
    GPT-4o passed about 61% of tau-bench's retail tasks on one try, but under 25% when every one of several tries had to pass. R
    More numbers
    Several tries here means eight in a row. 7.8% of SWE-bench patches marked resolved fail the full test suite. R
    6. 
    
  6. 06
    Human review is the bottleneck
    Speed-ups are mostly self-reported, and people overestimate them.
    In METR's randomized trial, experienced developers were 19% slower with early-2025 AI tools while believing they were 20% faster. R
    More numbers
    DORA 2025: 90% use AI; it goes with higher throughput and still with more instability. P
    7. 
  


  
Pick the shape by the task

  

    

      
Task shapeShape that held upEvidence

      
        
Many independent, read-heavy partsA lead with read-only helpers and a central coordinatorAnthropic's research system won by 90.2% on breadth-first research P

        
Steps with shared state (most feature work)One agent writes; helpers only read or reviewMulti-agent lost 39–70% on sequential planning R; Cognition keeps writes single-threaded P

        
A large mechanical change across many filesA scripted pipeline; the model edits; checks gate every fileAirbnb, Google, Spotify; Uber's batch AI migration failed P

        
Searching for a better solution with a machine scoreGenerate, score, keep the bestDeepMind's AlphaEvolve found a scheduling rule that recovers 0.7% of Google's fleet compute P

        
A judgment call with no testSample several answers and vote, or ask a fresh critic; a person decidesSelf-consistency added 17.9 points on a math benchmark R

      
    

  


  
Where reputable sources still disagree

  
    
    
  • Multiple agents. Anthropic's 2025 research system and Andrew Ng favor them P; Cognition, Thoughtworks, the MAST study and Google's study are skeptical for coding. Task shape explains most of the split.
    • 
    
  • Planning. Andrew Ng calls planning the least predictable pattern; Chip Huyen treats it as core and validates plans before running them. P
    • 
    
  • Humans in the loop. OpenAI's Codex team moved most review agent-to-agent P; Microsoft's Magentic-UI study raised success from 30.3% to 51.9% with human co-planning (a simulated user). R
    • 
  


  

    
What this means for your harness D

    
    
      
  • One writing agent by default; helpers read, search or review.
    • 
      
  • For big mechanical changes, script the pipeline and gate every file. Budget for the long tail.
    • 
      
  • Verification first. Don't count on self-critique without a test or checker.
    • 
      
  • Track all-runs pass rate and cost per task, not single wins.
    • 
      
  • Size agent output to what people can actually review.
    • 
    

  

  
Gathered by four research agents on 24 October 2026, mostly from paper abstracts, paper text and engineering posts. Spot-check a number against its source before quoting it. Biggest gap: no peer-reviewed, cost-matched comparison of orchestration setups on real coding work with current models, and almost no published defect or revert rates from industry.
